newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan hopes Russia will clear way for Siberian oil.
newsitem.headline: Japan hopes Russia will clear way for Siberian oil.

text.p: Japan and Russia may have shelved their territorial rifts to jump-start huge oil and gas projects in Russia's Far East, but Russian red tape at the regional and local levels still thwarts Japanese investment, industry sources say.

"If an improvement in economic relations can be fostered and pursued, it will ideally lead to a resolution of our political differences," said a Japan oil company executive who plans and develops projects in the oil-rich Sakhalin region off Russia's Pacific coast.
"But we would be very glad if legal improvements were made that bring to reality the promises of our existing oil and gas agreements," he said.

His comments preceded a visit to Tokyo next week by Russia's First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov and a delegation which will include Russian Central Bank Chairman Sergei Dubinin and Igor Farkhutdinov, the regionally powerful Head of Administration in Sakhalin.

Nemtsov, who also serves as Russia's Fuel and Energy Minister and has earned a reputation as a staunch proponent of reform, indicated on Tuesday in Moscow he would take a package of proposals to Tokyo to boost cooperation between the two countries and clear the way for energy deals.

Topping Japan's wish-list, Tokyo officials say, will be assurances that Sakhalin authorities will begin adhering to the taxation and tariff exemptions already guaranteed to Japanese companies by Moscow in their existing production sharing agreements (PSA).

"There is a lack of synthesised Russian policy trickling down to local levels, which still represents a hurdle to our efforts in the region," said an adviser to one of Japan's most active participants in Sakhalin.
"But we feel that Mr. Nemtsov is very interested in improving our conditions," he added.

Under existing Sakhalin production sharing agreements, guaranteed personally by Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin last June, companies are responsible only for taxes on profits, if and when oil starts flowing, a Japan oil industry executive said.

"But regional officials are either unaware of or often choose not to recognise this fact, and so we face a whole realm of difficulties in our operations from taxation and customs officials," he added.

The region has two major production-sharing oil and gas deals in initial stages: the $12 billion Sakhalin-I and $10 billion Sakhalin II projects. The former, whose three deposits are said to boast reserves of some 2.5 billion barrels of crude oil and over 15 trillion cubic feet of natural gas, is expected to begin production around 2001 to 2002.
Three appraisal wells will be drilled this month and operate through September, when the region is clear of ice, officials said.

Japanese companies in the international consortia conducting the projects include the Sakhalin Oil and Gas Development Co Ltd, a group comprised of the semi-governmental Japan National Oil Company and 13 other private Japanese firms. Trade houses Mitsui & Co Ltd and Mitsubishi Corp are also involved in the projects.
The Russian delegation's visit follows a trip to Moscow in late May by Japan Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda.
The two countries have been wrangling for decades over four small islands off the coast of Hokkaido in the north Pacific that were seized by Russia shortly after World War Two.
